segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s who’s gonna preach to us on our revival night next Monday night. Starting Monday night through Thursday, we’re going to be having good church service.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man, I’ll might come see y’all one night.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: OK, thank you, come see us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Charlie was telling me that they’re going to be eating wild onion Sunday at Belfonte.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Oh yeah… I don’t know, Charlie is going to be eating, he’s going to eat everything up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Somebody gave us some at church Sunday it didn’t last long. My wife cooked all up.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s good to eat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If we eat it one time, that’s good enough. Are you ready? It builds up. They record us talking. First off Sundown, we’re going to talk for a little while. They’ve already written what I’m supposed to ask you. I didn’t make these up. First of all, what is your name in English?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: In English? Sundown.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sundown.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Sundown Watie.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: S-ti-wi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: S-ti what is it?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: S-ti-wi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: S-ti-wi oh OK.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: S-ti-wi ohh-wee-ti.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ooh-wee-ti. Yeah, who gave that Cherokee name and what does it mean?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know if it means anything, but my dad named me that back then. My dad, he used to go to Colorado. They went cut the tip off the broom. Back then my mom was pregnant with me and my dad was thinking about what to name me. There was an Indian there that lived around there and was looking for him. He was thinking about it and he told him, “I don’t know what to name him.” He knew that I was going to be a boy and he told him, “Name him Sundown.” So that’s why my dad named me Sundown and he named me S-ti-wi in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about where was you born at?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A lot of them came here. A lot came here at the old building and we talked to them.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it was there in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What year?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: 1954 was the year I was born.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you grew up at?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I grew up in Bell and towards Salem. Mostly around Salem community, that’s where I grew up. That’s where I tried to go to school at Bell School.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Big school.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Big school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You must’ve gotten to know a lot of people?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: There were a lot of kids back then, and there were a lot of teenagers. There’s still a lot of them right now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You know them?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah. A lot of them has passed on.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, when I traveled around that way, I got to know a lot of y’all.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: When I first got to know you, do you remember when we was all working with DJ Francis?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s when I got to know you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it? We was helping the children out when they was needing something. We gave them something to get stuff at Walmart.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s when I came to know you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s been a few years now.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s been a long time. That was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it still going?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s still going, but I don’t know who’s doing it. I don’t know who’s doing it now. They still get letters. My wife still gets them, and she gives them out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, to the children that are in need?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: But I don’t know who’s doing it. The last one I knew that was doing it was Imogene Cochran that lived close by, but I don’t think it’s her anymore, it’s somebody else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Who was it that I talked to, said there’s still a program to help children in need. I think their name was Gorden. They were with the Johnsons.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know him either. I’ve seen him around, but I don’t know him all that well. If he’s there that’s great to help the children out.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time, I remember when we helped his mom up north. He said, “I sure do appreciate y’all.” It was almost time for the kids to start back school. “I appreciate y’all,” he said. I told him, “It’s not me, it’s God. We can’t do anything, but we have to get some clothes.”

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s what they say around Cherry Tree, even the kids. When my wife gets those papers, they fill them out. When they get those, they come to the house and ask for them. That’s what they understand, who gave it to them, and what other people are talking about, and other people come over to the house, looking for the papers. She tells them, “I’ll ask the main person and I will get some more.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to come to the house, around nine or ten be knocking on the door.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I’m glad, I don’t mind if she helps them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When we first moved to Steely there were some teenagers and they were driving pretty cars – had shiny wheels on them. I used to think, “That’s how they must be.” But the longer we stayed I saw kids that wasn’t living all that good. There are some kids that aren’t doing that well. One time a van pulled up and three of them got out, an older boy, a girl, and a younger boy. They got out, I said, “siyo,” that’s what I say to them and I said, “How you guys doing?” They didn’t say anything, then after a while, we had snacks that we gave them. Then I asked them, “What are your parents’ names?” and they told me. I said to them, “Maybe they might come later on.” The older one said, “I don’t know.” I didn’t know they could speak English. “My dad has been gone for a week and my mom has been gone since Friday. She went to go do laundry and she never came back and it’s Sunday.” They were in a sad situation. So that’s where you grew up at. Where you lived at, you didn’t live nowhere else?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: No, I just grew up there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you work at?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I worked at… I was still very young. I was still going to school. I was probably in the seventh grade. There was a chicken-catching crew. I didn’t go all the time. One day out of the week, maybe two. I was in the seventh grade and I was already working. I didn’t hardly go to school ‘cause I was working, trying to help my mom out. So, that’s what I did growing up there, working hard. From what I remember, it was hard. I would go to school. Sometimes I would go for a week. Then, when it came to work, I would go a couple nights. Sometimes when I got back home from work, I would go to school. I would fall asleep in school 'cause I was working nights catching chickens.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, they say that was some work.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s where I worked the most, nowhere else. I worked a couple of places for just a little while. I worked at the Stilwell High School when they was building it for about a year and then the road going towards Sallisaw, going up that big hill.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I worked there for a little while, and my brother was a crew boss for the chicken catchers. I was home one time, and he asked me, “Do you want to go to work?” And I was already working. I just quit and went catching chickens again. And all that time all together I started from Ft. Smith working two days, three days. All that I worked. I caught chickens for 47 years, the longest was at Decatur. I caught chickens 30 plus years, nowhere else. My arms are broke nowadays. They make noise all the time. I’m glad I can still use them – I thank God, too, for all he has done for me and that I can still move around. A lot of them ones I started doing that with, some of them don’t have legs and their backs are broken. I just thank God now, for how much he has watched over me. That’s hard work and it’s dirty work, too. Most of them inhaled the dust, but I had a mask on all the time and the ones that didn’t do that are doing dialysis. Some of them don’t have legs. I guess the dust is too strong where they inhaled it. My oldest brother, we used to work together and he’s doing dialysis now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I hear people that I know talking about it, that it’s a hard job to do. When was it that he was in here? I forget how many he said they hold in one hand.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: When I started, we was carrying 12.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee man.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Some of their hands were like this. Mine never got like that. That’s how many we was carrying and we was walking and putting them in the truck. It’s easy now, they have what they call loaders. They go inside and put the cages in.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s close by?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s close, but they still have to carry that many and put them in there. Back then that’s how many we carried but they lowered it to 10 to 11. They just kept lowering it, 'cause the chickens were big. Now they put seven in. It’s hard, dirty, and muddy, we was working and it stunk. We still went even, when it was snowing and raining. That’s what I went through for 47 years. They told me they was going to give me something when we was working in Decatur. They gave me a ring and a sweatshirt for working that long. I thought they was going to give me money. I still have that ring and sweatshirt. I got it hanging up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You haven’t worked with 5-O?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, we’ve worked together. Boy, there’s a lot of boys that we worked together are still alive. Some are still here and some of them are passed on.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: 5-0 used to say that. How many of y’all are in the family?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Four of us – five of us, really. We adopted one little boy, but we raised him just the same. There was five of us. One of my brothers – you know Dora Mae?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They were married and his kidneys went bad and he passed away, too, and it’s the same with the oldest. He’s on dialysis, too. And my daughter was the same. She passed away, too. The other ones are OK and Phil, that’s my brother. You know Phil?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s your brother?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dora Mae. She’s the organizer of the WMU.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I went and preached to them a while back.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, she was telling about it. It’s going good, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it? That’s good. What was your parents' names?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: My mom's name was E-tse. Ada, her name was Ada. Ada Watie was her name in English. E-tse in Cherokee. Yeah, Ada Watie and in Cherokee it was E-tse.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you know what that means? Ada Watie?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I really don’t know what that means. It would’ve been good if I paid attention to what it meant or if I asked her. I never paid attention to what it meant. It probably means something though. E-tse I don’t know what it means.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, we was saying a long time ago. People that lived a long time ago, they were getting their names. They were naming their kids, and they were getting names from the Bible. What was your dad's name?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Dewi. His name was Dewi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Are they both gone?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They’re both gone. They been gone for a long time now, both of them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did they live?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They lived in Salem.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Both of them?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah. My mom was the only one who grew up in Greasy. Do you know them, Glass?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Which ones?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: What is that man's name? I forget his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were they kin to Raymond?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, they were kin. Yeah, we’re kin to Raymond Glass. We’re real close family. Yeah, they grew up towards Salem. Yeah, like my dad down Sally Bull Hollow – have you heard of it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah, I’ve heard them talking about it.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Way down there, past Four Vision Church, that’s where my dad grew up at and my mom says she grew up around Greasy. So, when they got together, they went that way. We grew up in Salem.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went down Sally Bull Hollow, you’re talking about. One time they called me at Four Vision to go preach. I barely found it.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s a long ways. All them boys that live down there, we’re all cousins. Them Sawneys. You know them, don’t you? All them Sawneys that live down there, we’re all cousins and... what’s their names? Them Greens, we’re all cousins. There’s a lot of boys that live down there that don’t know God. A lot of them, we’re cousins. Them Sawneys, they just really grew up there. They didn’t even go to town. When they grew up, that’s when they got out. Started going to town. They didn’t know what it was like. That’s how it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you take them?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: No, I didn’t, but we got together when they got used to coming to town. We got together sometimes. We weren’t together all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was asking this one person from that way – his name was Sawney – if he was kin to Aleg Sawney – do you know him? He was short. He was a preacher.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Aleg Sawney, I didn’t know him. I’ve heard of that name you’re talking about Aleg Sawney.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That one time...who was it that I was talking to? I was talking to a white person. We was talking about Aleg Sawney. I told him, “He’s the only one that really looks up to me.” He said, “Really?” I said, “Yeah – he was just this tall!”

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: He was looking up! Looking at you. Gah-lee, oh my goodness! If you would have made him mad, y’all would’ve made some noise there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, your parents just lived around there?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, they just grew up around there. And them Livers – you know them, don’t you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, a few of them.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Them, we’re close cousins, them Livers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That one – what is his name? He's a welder, a Livers?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Johnny Ray’s son. Johnny Ray and...what is his name? I know his name. Yeah, they’re close cousins.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I used to see them around when we gathered at the Livers.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: We’re all cousins.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about...what do they say... clan? Their clan? Cherokees call it ‘clan’. Do you know what clan you’re in? Clan.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know what that is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know either.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Me either. I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Long time ago they say y’all were in the clan, but I don’t know.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know that, either.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about your parents’ parents, like your grandma? What were their names?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They called my grandma, I-tsa-gi my grandma. And they called my grandpa, Johnson. That I know. They used to call her I-tsa-gi u-ta-na. She was only this tall, but my grandpa was tall. Johnson, they used to call him. Johnson u-we-ti.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was real tall.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: He was real tall and skinny. He was tall and my grandma was short and they was still calling her big. They grew up from there. They used to live in Sally Bull, way up there on top of the mountain. It’s just like this. That road is still there. I went over there the other day. I went and seen one of his wives who’d passed away. That’s where I seen that road. It’s just like this, like a snake all the way to where they used to live. They lived by the rocks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they live by themselves?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: His sons used to live there back then, but all of his sons are passed on. None of them are alive now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s just empty now?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s empty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about seeing the area, does it still look the same?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: It’s a real wooded area where they used to live. I asked one boy and he said you can only get halfway to where they used to live from the road. The road is all messed up. Nobody don’t live down that way. The road got all tore up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is their house still there?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: No, it burned down. It was old. It looks pretty where they used to live back then. My dad had a big fence where he had pigs in there. There was water coming out of the rocks. There was a pipe coming out of the rocks. They were getting water there, and it was cold. It never went away. I was asking that one if it was still coming out, and he said it was still coming out. I don’t know if the pipe is still there. It was this big where it came out. We was going all the way up there to get water. We had a little trail. They had rocks – you probably seen the big rocks they had? It had holes in them for dogs to eat and drink water. I was wanting to go look for them, but I don’t know if they’re still there and I don’t know who to ask to go through there. He said that’s as far as the road goes. He said it’s all tore up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back then there was some pretty springs coming out.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, they were clean back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There’s some elders back where I pastor at Steely, they talk about how they had a road close by and there was a mountain on the side of it and there was water coming out of it. One time we went back – I forget when it was – it was all thicket, but it was still coming out. It was beautiful coming out, but it was real thicket in there.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s how it is where they used to live. You can tell there was a house there but it’s real thicket and briars there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes you take flowers where they used to live? How about your parents, we talked about it a while ago. Where did they meet when they first got to know each other?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Boy, that one I don’t know. Where they meet, I really don’t know. I would say… I guess I really don’t know. They never said anything about it. My mom never told us about it, how they meet.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They never told me either. They might be keeping it a secret. How about you? I think we talked about it a while ago, your last name. Your name is Watie. Did they ever tell you where the name Watie came from?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I really don’t. I don’t ever remember where that started and where my last name came from. They might have talked about it and I just didn’t listen. I don’t know. My mom never told me anything about it before where it came from. Her brother’s name was Da-sa-ti.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was Da-sa-ti?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was the meaning of that?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know what it meant, Da-sa-ti. They lived in Greasy. That’s where she was from. That’s where she lived. You know Mike Glass?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t think I know him.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: He went to school here at Sequoyah. That was his son Da-sa-ti. Yeah, Da-sa-ti Mike Glass. I guess you can call them my first cousins, since that was my mom's sister.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, some tell some amazing stories when they tell where their last name came from.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I never knew where my last name came from. I don’t know where it came from.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: From what they told me... My last name is Soldier. When it started a long time ago, when they was giving land to them, they say our last name was Glory, but they say later on they changed it to Soldier. I don’t know if it’s true, that’s what they just say. I just thought you might know something like that.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I don’t know anything like that or don’t remember them talking about anything like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What we was really saying... We was talking about it when they was giving land a long time ago. They changed their names, but that wasn’t their names. Then again some of them didn’t know their last names. They were just giving to them. Do they just call you Sundown?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah. The other ones call me St-ew, by my Cherokee name but most of the people I go to church with call by my English name. I don’t know if they know my Cherokee name. I keep it a secret. Yeah, most of them from that way call me St-ew.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They call me Ooh-yo-s-gi. One time I used to care for an elder lady. That old lady liked to joke around. When she became ill, they asked for us to go get her our pastor and she said “No he’s always hungry”. I always ask them when I go visit people, “What y’all got on the table?” But I just joke around with them. How about your parents, did they ever tell that they saw something amazing? Something that they saw happening?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They would talk about booger man long time. I know one that my mom would talk about. There used to be an old lady, but I don’t know her name. They used to say she was a shapeshifter – you could see her. We wasn’t that far apart. We could see her flying sometimes and she would go under. Sometimes we would go over there and whenever we knocked, she opened. When it would start getting dark, I don’t know if it was from the cherries and ashes. She threw out, but she would be messing around with it. I don’t know if she was shapeshifting, but that’s what she would be doing. Stirring up the ashes, and if something happened, she would fly away. And whichever way she went, there would be an owl hooting. She said, “I saw her myself, she would be flying, and she would go underneath.” I think that’s amazing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s really amazing, them seeing that a long time ago. They was telling me one time... what do they call them, thunderbirds?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Raven Mocker.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were around. They say they were the meanest ones.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They say they go everywhere.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Something like that, let’s say like, the maggots – I don’t know if you’ve ever heard of the fly? The green fly, it’ll lay eggs real quick if there’s something. You’ve seen them, haven’t you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I think so.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They say if there’s one flying around in the house and if you kill it, that’s what they was telling me, this one guy, them Livers was telling me. He said, “A green fly was bothering us at night, flying around.” And when he killed it, he threw it in the fire and the next morning a man came over and he had burns on him. I don’t know if it was him, but he had burns all over him. He came to beg for something. He said, “If you don’t give him what he’s begging for, he would end up dying.” That was something amazing I heard of. That’s what that Livers guy was telling me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When we was growing up, me and my sister would be playing outside and when it got dark sometimes we’d still be out there playing. Our mom would tell us to come in. “Something is going to join y’all!” But one time we didn’t listen. There was three of us. After a while we went inside real quick.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s what we were told, too. They would say, “Something’s going to join y’all.” That’s what they told me, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I think about it, I believe that it was true. They knew… There were some living back then.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, they were living back then. They were strong, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What we was talking about, those thunderbirds, there were some living.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They say those were the real bad ones. I’ve heard them say that before.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Especially when someone was sick real bad. That’s when they would be flying around.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They would be making sounds like an owl or a bird. I guess that’s what it was, acting like it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was telling my friends one time, we was south of Jay one night. We was drinking, too, and talking about stuff. We was standing outside and it was at night. After a while we heard an owl on this side. It hooted again and the third time it hooted, it coughed! One of the boys that was with us said, “Hey, just go back home.”

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: So, it coughed, huh?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we rolled around roughly laughing. One of the boys told it, “Just go back home.”

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Gah-lee…They saw stuff long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they saw stuff. One of the elders was telling me it’s a good thing I didn’t learn what he was teaching me. He said if a booger man is visiting you, you’re supposed to do this. If it gets close to you, you can recognize it. There will be a shadow of who it is. I never wanted to see, but if someone appeared and if they saw you the next day, they would be ashamed. They wouldn’t even look at you. They would just have their head down. They say it’s real scary.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it was. They saw some real scary stuff. That was really happening what they saw.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Someone was telling me, one time they had a .22. He said there was an owl hooting. He said he went and got it. Some of them knew how to put medicine on a bullet. If it’s hooting over there, it would be over here. When you shoot, shoot it this way a little bit. He shot that .22 then after a while, it fell off. It was hooting this way, but it fell off on this side. That’s what I was taught, how to make medicine for a bullet. Later on, a man came over. Boy, he had scars on his back and on his butt cheeks. He said he came looking for me to heal him.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: All shot up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They tell some great stories. How about your grandma, did they ever tell you about when the Cherokees came from North Carolina a long time ago? Did they ever tell anything about what happened along the way?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They never said anything, just that they went through poorly. How bad they got treated, that’s all they told. All they would say was it was really bad. They never would say any more about it. That’s what they would say, “It was real bad.” They would say they hid deep under the rocks to sleep, that’s all they would say. They wouldn’t say any more about it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn’t want to say how bad they went through it and how poorly it was. We talked to this one old lady, I mean the one she raised. The old lady was 114 years old when she died, some of them was telling us, the one who told us. And they’re thinking she’s 114 years old, but the old lady was really 140 years old. It’s the same as her wisdom or when she was born or if her parents told her how they came through. They told some amazing stories.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, really back then they lived a long time and now not so much. They might pass at 90 or a little bit over 100.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back then, we used to say they were walking and things, living in the woods.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They was eating stuff. Me, back then where we live at right now, that house where my mom used to live, we would walk from there to Salem Church at night. In the evening we would go. I’d say it’s about five miles. Walking from Salem to my mom's it could be three, when they went to go visit in Sally Bull. We had trails in the woods, you could come out at Bell. We had trails to go visit each other for a week.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s how it was back then.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Nowadays they don’t want you to come. They won’t allow you to spend the night.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Or they’ll meet you on the porch.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, they won’t tell you to come in. They’ll bring a chair out on the porch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Them dogs would come lay down and be scratching. How about what we was talking about while ago? What was it like where you lived and grew up at? What was it like to look around?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Nowadays, they got fields. It wasn’t like that. Like, my house, it was just woods close by. I used to hunt. I was just a little boy when I started hunting. It was beautiful everywhere. Nobody had no-hunting signs posted. You could go anywhere. You could hunt anywhere back then. Now it’s not like that. Now, back where I grew up at, in front where it was all woods, now there’s a field. It’s not like that anymore. They don’t allow you to go in. I hunted that whole mountain in Bell. When I was a little boy my dad gave me a gun, a .410. I still have that gun. That’s what I used. I was hunting squirrels. That’s how it was back then. I was fishing in them creeks. They were beautiful back then. Now they’ve all changed and all tore up. Where I used to fish and swim you can’t swim anymore. It’s just this deep. They’re all tore up. Where I grew up, even the roads have changed their highways. A lot of us would walk on the roads when we was kids. They came from different places, and we would meet up somewhere on the road and play. That’s how we were growing up going to school. We would come down whenever they said to meet there or they would come up. That’s how it was back then, when we played.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Everything has changed nowadays. They got fences.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They have fences everywhere. You can’t go anywhere. It was a good place to hunt back then, even to look around. You could even find peaches, apples, persimmons, and grapes. You could find a lot of different things back then. Now you can’t find anything. They tore everything up. That’s what we ate, or we’d bring them back with us to our house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s really like that, 'cause nowadays they closed off the swimming places.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Boy, they definitely do have them closed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about how many people lived close by where you grew up at?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Where I grew up at, there were three houses. White people, us Cherokees were in the middle, white people – lived in three houses. One of them was a teacher at Stilwell. He was the principal. His name was Bill Catcher. Kids live there. His kids, his oldest kid’s kid live there where he lived. They built a house behind them. There’s more houses there now. There ain’t just three houses there. On this side, Willard Catcher used to live there and children. There’s other people living there. There are more houses there, close by and on this side are the Starrs. The Starrs took over. They took the place that I used to hunt. They made a field. There’s a lot more houses there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A lot more?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They logged everywhere out where I used to hunt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you wave at each other sometimes when y’all see each other?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: We do, they’re real nice them Starrs. I mean to talk to, I mean I don’t know if they’ll allow you to go in. And them Catchers… That Willard Catcher, he passed a long time ago. I don’t know what happened to his kids. Other people are living there. They’re real nice, too. Their name is Wallace.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s real good if they’re nice.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: They watch my brother. Like if he wants something, they’ll come over. If he needs something. That’s how they are. They’re good people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time the Sharps had land south of Jay. Do you know Brush Creek?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, I know where it’s at, or Pritchett.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It all belonged to the Cherokees. One time, white people from the east came and bought it and put a fence up. Them Sharps had a swimming hole. I forget what they call it. They might call it rocks sticking in water and when the white people bought it and when the Sharps went swimming, they got chased off. They got shot at with a gun. Later on, there was some white boys coming. There was a gate and where the gate was, it was our land. The Sharps and them boys were coming. There was a quite a few of them Sharps boys. When they seen them white boys coming, he said, “We started going that way, too. We didn’t let them come out.” He said, “We were staring at each other rough. We thought, ‘we can throw down if they want to, too’.” They turned around and said, “We’re going to go tell our parents.” Their parents were real rich and the Sharps parents came and talked to them, and they worked it out and they let us get in and out.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Where I’m living at, I don’t know what you would call them. I guess you could call them Japanese.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, Asians.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, just behind the house, by the mountain, just behind there, the green houses. I used to hunt there, but they logged it. There ain’t no place for me to hunt. There still is a place but not that much. They logged where it was a good place and they got a big field and that’s where they built the green houses.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s where they’re selling them. That’s where they’re growing them.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: The man that sold it lived there and owned the mountain. And when they sold it to him, that road, they made him make a different road. That road he had to get to it, they wouldn’t let him get to it. They made him make a different road. That’s what they did. They have a lot of houses there Fog Holler Road. I don’t know if you ever been through there? They call it Fog Holler. Go through Bethel Church on Fog Holler Road, you can come out at Salem. When you go through the mountain, you can see it when you get on top.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That road that goes towards Kenwood. They’re growing that stuff you smoke. They got big fences where they’re hiding it.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: A lot of them have it like that – by Cherry Tree, by the church, by the airport. Oh man, they have a lot of houses right by the church, about a mile from the airport.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time I asked a woman, an old woman, she went to church at Steely. I said, “How come you’re this way?” She said, “Haw.” I asked, “What’s wrong?” She said somebody flies a helicopter and there was a field by her house. “Boy, sometimes,” she was saying. “Haw, sometimes it lands. It comes down. Them boys go stand by. They throw that hay-like grass. It don’t stay one minute, then it flies again. That’s why it was flying away. There’s a lot of them around.”

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s everywhere now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where you grew up at, you don’t ever remember anything about where you grew up at? You don’t see anything good where you grew up at, how it was?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: What I remember, if I remember something about what my mom said to me and told me what to do, I think to myself it would have been good if I had only listened. She would tell, “You’re going to learn. Go to school. It is important.” She would tell, “One day, you are going to need it.” If I had just obeyed her, I would have been good and I would have learned something. I mean, really, I don’t know anything. But I’m glad I can write my name. I know that much. I think it would have been good if I had listened to her tell me something. I’m thankful that I can still do that. “And remember,” I think to myself, “It would have been good.” Now I tell our kids to do it. I push them. I tell them, “Don’t be like me. Go to school. It will be better for y’all.” I tell my grandkids the same thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your wife went to school?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, she went to school and finished twelfth grade. She went to college for a little while. Back then it was hard for them to go, moneywise and transportation but, yeah, she went to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays if anyone is wanting to go to school, Cherokee Nation is willing to help them. Or if they can find something different, 'cause it was really hard back when we was growing up.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: All the boys that I went to school with, that’s just how we were. We were going to school, but some of us wasn’t going in. We was running off into the woods and when they was about to let out, we would come out. I think sometimes it would have been good if I didn’t do that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One of my friends – he’s not alive anymore, but he was my friend – someone asked us, “How come y’all are going to school?” We told, “I guess 'cause we’re hungry.” I told him, “We just come to eat.” How about now? Let’s say food. What did your parents cook that y’all liked what your mom made, like pie or something different?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Chicken. Chicken and dumplings, fried potatoes. Onion and boiled potatoes and pies, apple pies and strawberry pies and cobbler. It was strawberry, they called it cobbler and cake. She always made a cake for me on my birthday. Coconut. She mixed it herself. It was homemade. It was white and sprinkled with coconut. It would be sitting pretty, it would be this thick. That’s what I miss and those biscuits. My partner can make some biscuits, but they will never turn out like how your mom made them. They’re good, and gravy water gravy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What are you calling that?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Water gravy made by water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me and my wife like that. When we’re by ourselves, we tear it up.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Boy, when I’m by myself sometimes, I make that. Just different things like rabbit. When I boil it, I use that soup. Same with squirrel. That’s what Mom used to do if I killed a wild turkey. I’d tell her, “Mom cook this, make gravy with it.” She would make it with that gravy, with that soup. It was good. That’s what I miss.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your wife don’t make it?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: No, she can’t cook. She’ll make gravy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Not that good.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: No, I’m afraid to eat it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You’re probably afraid to tell her, too. How about towards the end…The Cherokee we are speaking now and these kids that are going to school to learn how to speak Cherokee [phone ringing] These kids that are going to school, the sound of them speaking Cherokee and how we speak. It is a little different than how we speak it.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: It’s different now. I can tell if someone learned how to speak it, it sounds different.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you talk to someone that went to school here, do you understand what they are saying?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I have to listen to them and ask them what they are saying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you understand them after that?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Yeah, you have to listen to them real good, to what they are saying. Sometimes I’ll ask them, “What are you saying?” And when he says it again I hear it. Like how I would speak it and understand it. Just how they speak it, it’s clear that they are just now learning.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You can tell right away.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Even my kids, my girls they don’t speak Cherokee and when they try to say what I’m saying, it sounds different. They’ll say it different, but they understand it a little bit. Sometimes my grandson, it’ll sound pretty, just like how I sound. It’ll sound like that. I tell him, “You can learn real easy how to speak it if you pay attention.” But they’re embarrassed to try to talk. I don’t know why they’re embarrassed to talk. That one boy Ronnie Duncan – I don’t know if y’all know him – his name is Ronnie Duncan. He comes over to my house and asks me, “How do you say this? How do you say this?” And he’s Cherokee. He said, “I wish I would have learned it.” I was telling him how he said it and how to say it. He asked me to teach him how to pray. They were going to North Carolina riding bicycles. He said they asked me to pray in Cherokee, but I don’t know how. I told him what to say. “Just say it like this.” He was trying. I was teaching him. He learned it, so I guess he prayed when they left.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What’s his name?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Ronnie Duncan.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Ronnie Duncan? My daughter used to take those bicycle riders. I just thought I’d ask. I know them people.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s what he was asking. He’ll come over to the house sometimes when he’s asking something. “What’s this? What’s this?” – saying something like that. And we tell him, me and my wife, what it is. Sometimes when I tell him something, it makes it harder for him to say what I’m saying and my wife makes it easier. “Say it this way. It is easier or it’ll be shorter.” I guess I’m more Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time, my wife was teaching the missionaries. They were going overseas somewhere. They was wanting to know what to do to speak a different language, but she was teaching them Cherokee. He asked, “How do you say these cheeks?” I told him. “Ti-qui-li ti-qui-li. Say it again.” He done this and looked at me, “ti-qua-li.” I wanted to laugh, but my wife wouldn’t let me. They kind of sound the same, ‘ti-qua-li’ and ‘ti-qui-li’. I sure did want to laugh, but I didn’t laugh.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: Ti-qua-li.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re finishing up now, Sundown. We might have went over. These that are going to school, what do you think – deep inside, what do you think? Is it going to stay the Cherokee language after we’re gone here? Where they’re going to school at?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: If we really have to say, I think it’s going to run out. It’s good that they’re going to school. I like it. I would like for my kids to learn Cherokee. I would like that, 'cause if it ain’t for that, it’s going to run out. I’m glad that they are teaching them and they are learning.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s going to be joyful if they use it.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: It’s going to be joyful if they keep going and if they use it and if they understand it 'cause people nowadays, like the elders, they don’t understand English and they can help them out real good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s real joyful that non Cherokees want to learn Cherokee.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: A lot of them want to learn. The real Cherokees don’t want to.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Tell him about that one white person that came over.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The other day a white person came over and he wasn’t even part Cherokee. We was in the office. We talked – boy he talked pretty Cherokee! He was talking just like me and you are, a white person. He wasn’t even part Cherokee.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He saw it somewhere where they were talking Cherokee and he wanted to learn and he really learned it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, he wasn’t missing nothing. He was talking just like how me and you are.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: That’s good. It’s good if it’s like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He wasn’t even part Cherokee, not even a little bit.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He was from Chicago.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: When I was growing up, that Catcher I was talking about, he lives there. He still lives there. We used to play around. He was older, boy, he was probably 15 and I was probably eight. He learned Cherokee while we was playing around 'cause I didn’t speak English. I spoke Cherokee and a little English. I was using Cherokee and he understood what I was saying and he kept learning. We was talking in Cherokee. He’s forgotten all of it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He don’t speak it no more?

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: He forgot all of it. That’s really joyful, I’m glad they’re doing that learning and want to. If it wasn’t for that, there would be a little Cherokee and now it’s growing I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m glad that we are fighting to keep the Cherokee language. I’m scared to lose it. In North Carolina they say there are only a few Cherokee speakers left. It’s going down.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: It’s different too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, Sundown, I’m glad.

segments.speaker: sundown-watie
segments.translation: I am, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m glad.
